screens.title: Managing Compute (Nova) and Image (Glance) Services
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how Nova and Glance work together to deliver virtual machines from trusted templates. Nova orchestrates the lifecycle of instances — booting, stopping, and terminating — while Glance stores the disk images that we use as templates. You will see concrete commands for creating flavors, uploading SSH key pairs, defining security group rules, and importing images into Glance. Knowing how to design flavors and manage image formats matters because flavors determine runtime resource allocation and images determine boot behavior and security posture. A mis-sized flavor wastes host resources, and a stale image can expose vulnerabilities. Throughout the lesson you will practice common CLI patterns and a reproducible workflow for launching a secure web server instance. Expect hands-on examples that show how to create a custom flavor, add a key pair, open SSH and HTTP in a security group, and upload a QCOW2 image. By the end you should be able to reason about instance sizing, secure access, and image hygiene. Consider: what would change for a database workload versus a web workload when you pick a flavor and image?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Managing Compute & Image
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Managing Compute (Nova) and Image (Glance) Services

Provision virtual machines from trusted images, define flavors that match workload needs, secure access with key pairs and security groups, and keep image inventories clean and safe.

In this lesson • Terminal-first demo • Hands-on activity
Orientation

You will follow a repeatable flow: confirm or upload an image to Glance, create a flavor that fits your workload, add a key pair for SSH, open only the needed ports with a security group, then boot an instance and verify networking. These steps form the production-safe path to launching an instance.

Why it matters
  • Right-sized flavors reduce contention and cost.
  • Key pairs avoid password-based attacks.
  • Image hygiene reduces attack surface.
Explore Key Topics
Flavors & Sizing
Design flavors to match CPU, RAM and disk needs; avoid overcommit surprises.
Secure Access
Use SSH key pairs and minimal security group rules to limit exposure.
Image Hygiene
Prefer QCOW2 with cloud-init and purge unneeded packages before snapshotting.
Concept Map
How Nova and Glance connect
Glance
Image repository
Stores QCOW2 and RAW images used to boot instances. Images can be public or private per project.
Nova
Instance lifecycle
Nova uses images, flavors, key pairs and security groups to boot and manage instances for tenants.
Flavor
Virtual hardware profile
Defines CPU, RAM, and disk sizes. Create custom flavors to match workload profiles.
Quick start checklist
  • Confirm or upload your image to Glance.
  • Create or choose a flavor aligned with your workload.
  • Create a key pair for SSH and a narrow security group for ports.

screens.title: Nova: compute lifecycle and responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: Nova is the OpenStack service responsible for managing virtual machine instances and their lifecycle from boot to termination. Concretely, Nova coordinates resource allocation on hypervisors, tracks instance metadata, and exposes CLI commands to create, rebuild, resize, shelve, pause, and delete instances. This responsibility matters because instance lifecycle operations interact with other services: images from Glance define the disk template, networks provide addresses, and block storage attaches volumes. A common misconception is that Nova alone provides disk contents; in reality Nova consumes images from Glance when booting and delegates the image lifecycle to Glance. For example, when you run a server create command, Nova requests the image, schedules the instance on a compute node that has capacity according to the flavor, injects the SSH key if provided, and applies security group rules. An example claim: booting a web server from a QCOW2 image with a custom flavor and injected key pair should produce a reachable instance that reports the expected C P U and memory. Misunderstandings often arise when users expect instance disk contents to be updated when the Glance image changes — that does not happen automatically; snapshots or rebuilds are required. Takeaway: Nova runs the lifecycle but relies on images, flavors, and network security to produce a usable instance. How will you confirm scheduling and resource allocation when you boot a test VM?

keyIdea.title: Nova in one line
keyIdea.text: Nova orchestrates instance creation and lifecycle, using flavors for resources and Glance images for boot disks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Nova Lifecycle
Definition
Nova manages compute resources and the lifecycle of instances. It schedules instances to compute nodes and coordinates with Glance, Neutron, and Cinder for images, networking, and block storage.
Common operations
  • Boot: create a new instance from an image and flavor.
  • Rebuild: replace the disk with another image and reboot.
  • Resize: change the instance flavor and resources.
  • Terminate: remove instance and free resources.
Key Takeaway

Nova controls instance lifecycle but depends on external services for images, networking and storage.

Example flow
When you run a server create command, Nova: requests the image from Glance, selects a host based on flavor and capacity, injects the SSH public key if provided, and applies security group rules. The instance then boots and registers its state in Nova.
Concrete example
Boot a tiny instance for testing, then use openstack server show to confirm host and flavor were honored.
Misconception
Changing a Glance image does not change already-running instances. To update running systems, rebuild or snapshot and relaunch from the updated image.

screens.title: Flavors: default vs custom sizing
screens.narratorSegment: Flavors are named profiles that define virtual hardware for an instance: vCPU count, R A M size, and root disk size. OpenStack ships with defaults such as m1. tiny and m1. small, but production workloads often require custom flavors tuned to their needs. For example, a database server typically needs more R A M and possibly dedicated C P U, while a stateless web server can use a smaller flavor with shared C P U. When designing flavors you must map virtual resources to physical host capabilities so you do not overcommit beyond what the hypervisors and NUMA topology can support. A common mistake is creating flavors with resource sizes that cannot be satisfied by the compute fleet, leading to scheduling failures. Another misconception is treating flavors as billing labels only; in practice they directly influence performance and scheduling decisions. Concrete example: create a flavor named m1. medium-custom with 2 vCPUs, 4GB R A M and 40GB disk, then set hw:cpu_policy to dedicated if you need isolated CPUs. The practical takeaway is to standardize a small set of flavors that cover typical workloads, and document the performance expectations for each. How would you map an OLTP database requirement of high memory and moderate C P U to a flavor spec?

keyIdea.title: Design rule
keyIdea.text: Create flavors that reflect workload needs and physical host capacity; avoid creating many overlapping flavors to reduce sprawl.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Flavors
What a flavor defines
  • vCPU count
  • RAM in megabytes
  • Root disk size in gigabytes
  • Optional properties, e.g., hw:cpu_policy for dedicated CPUs
Comparison: default vs custom
Default
Quick to use but may not match production needs. Good for tests and CI tasks.
Custom
Tailored to workload; specify CPU policy and properties for performance-sensitive services.
Key Takeaway

Standardize a small set of documented flavors that align with common workloads and host capabilities.

Concrete example
openstack flavor create --ram 4096 --disk 40 --vcpus 2 m1.medium-custom
openstack flavor set --property hw:cpu_policy=dedicated m1.medium-custom
This creates a medium custom flavor and marks it for CPU dedication when supported by the host.
Misconception
Flavors are not access control labels; they determine resource allocation and scheduling, not tenancy or quota by name alone.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Create a Flavor
Walkthrough
Run the create command with desired RAM, disk, and vcpus. Use flavor set to attach properties like hw:cpu_policy. Always verify with flavor list and flavor show.
Pro tip
Maintain a short catalog that maps flavor names to workload types and expected performance so operators pick the correct flavor under pressure.
Key Takeaway

Create, annotate, and verify flavors; document their intended use.

Terminal
# Create a custom flavor for a medium-sized VM
openstack flavor create --ram 4096 --disk 40 --vcpus 2 m1.medium-custom
# Set a flavor property, for example to request dedicated CPUs
openstack flavor set --property hw:cpu_policy=dedicated m1.medium-custom
# Verify the flavor exists
openstack flavor list
openstack flavor show m1.medium-custom
Expected verification
  • Flavor appears in openstack flavor list.
  • openstack flavor show shows the hw:cpu_policy property if set.

screens.title: Key pairs: secure SSH access
screens.narratorSegment: Key pairs are a foundational way to secure SSH access to instances. Instead of using passwords, which are hard to rotate and easy to leak, you create an SSH key pair on your workstation and upload the public key to OpenStack. When you launch an instance with that key pair name, the public key is injected into the instance so you can SSH using your private key. The practical steps are: generate a key with ssh-keygen if you do not already have one; upload the public key using openstack keypair create --public-key path name; and list keys with openstack keypair list. A concrete example from the chapter uses ssh-keygen with RSA 2048 and uploads the resulting public key. A common mistake is not using the key pair name when launching the instance, or using the wrong private key when attempting to connect. Another pitfall is committing private keys to version control. After uploading, verify the key pair appears in the list and confirm the instance metadata shows the key name. Takeaway: key pairs enable automated, secure access without passwords. How will you ensure private key security when multiple operators need access?

keyIdea.title: Secure access rule
keyIdea.text: Always use SSH key pairs for automated and secure instance access; never distribute private keys in plaintext or version control.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Key Pairs
Why key pairs
Key pairs enable public-key authentication and remove the need to manage host passwords. They are suitable for automation and avoid weak credentials in production systems.
Best practices
  • Generate keys with strong algorithms and protect private keys with a passphrase if appropriate.
  • Do not store private keys in code repositories or shared drives.
  • Rotate keys if an operator leaves or a key is suspected compromised.
Key Takeaway

Use SSH key pairs for predictable and auditable access; verify key injection after booting an instance.

Commands
# Generate an SSH key pair
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 2048 -f ~/.ssh/my_openstack_key

# Upload the public key to OpenStack
openstack keypair create --public-key ~/.ssh/my_openstack_key.pub my_openstack_key

# List available key pairs
openstack keypair list
Verification
After launching, check instance metadata with openstack server show to see the key name. Attempt SSH using the private key and verify access is granted only with that key.

screens.title: Security groups: rules that protect instances
screens.narratorSegment: Security groups are stateful firewall rule collections applied to network interfaces of instances. They control what inbound and outbound traffic is allowed and are essential for isolating workloads and enforcing the principle of least privilege. A typical workflow is to create a security group for a role — for example web-servers — and then add rules to allow port 22 for SSH and port 80 for HTTP from required addresses. The chapter includes commands to create a security group and add rules for SSH and HTTP. A common mistake is forgetting to attach the security group to the instance or assuming the default group allows inbound traffic; often the default blocks incoming connections. Another pitfall is opening broad CIDR ranges unnecessarily. A concrete example: create web-servers, add rules for TCP 22 and 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 only if you need global access; otherwise lock to management networks. Finally, validate by checking openstack security group show and then testing connectivity. Consider whether a management jump host would reduce your exposure instead of allowing universal SSH access. Security groups: rules that protect instances means use narrowly scoped security group rules and attach groups intentionally to instances; avoid overly broad access ranges.. In practical terms, stateful firewalls and common rules for secure services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Security Groups
Create and add rules
openstack security group create web-servers
openstack security group rule create --protocol tcp --dst-port 22 --remote-ip 0.0.0.0/0 web-servers
openstack security group rule create --protocol tcp --dst-port 80 --remote-ip 0.0.0.0/0 web-servers
These commands create a web server security group and add SSH and HTTP rules. Replace 0.0.0.0/0 with a management CIDR when possible.
Validation
Use openstack security group show to inspect rules and openstack server show to confirm the security group is attached to the instance. Test connectivity from an allowed source.
Common Mistake

Forgetting to attach the newly created security group to the instance will keep the instance unreachable despite rules existing.

Analogy
Think of security groups as a per-instance stateful firewall. You apply the firewall to the network interface just like assigning a rule set to a server rack in a datacenter.
Concrete scenario
If a user cannot SSH in but the instance has a floating IP, inspect the instance security groups. If port 22 is missing, add the rule and re-test connectivity.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Booting an Instance
Full launch command
openstack server create --image "cirros" --flavor m1.tiny --key-name my_openstack_key --security-group web-servers my-web-instance
This single command uses the pre-existing cirros image, a tiny flavor, an uploaded key, and a web security group to boot my-web-instance.
Post-launch verification
  • openstack server list to see the instance and its status.
  • openstack server show my-web-instance to inspect assigned host, addresses, and key name.
  • Assign a floating IP if you need external access and test SSH/HTTP connectivity.
Key Takeaway

A successful boot requires image, flavor, key pair, and security rules to be prepared and referenced in the server create command.

Common mistake
If SSH fails even though the instance is active and has a floating IP, check the security group rules and the key-name used at launch first.
Concrete scenario
You launch a web server but a browser shows connection refused. Confirm HTTP rule exists in the security group and that the instance firewall is not blocking the port.

screens.title: SSH connectivity issues: diagnosis and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: When a user reports they cannot SSH into a running instance with a floating IP, the most common cause is security group rules blocking inbound SSH. Start your diagnosis by verifying that the instance is ACTIVE with openstack server show and that it has the expected floating IP. Next, list the security groups attached to the instance and inspect rules with openstack security group show. If port 22 is missing, add the rule and retry. Another possibility is that the wrong key pair was used at launch; confirm the key-name in the instance metadata and ensure the client is using the matching private key. Less common causes include the instance's internal firewall blocking SSH or cloud-init failing to inject the key at first boot. Always check cloud-init logs inside the instance when possible. A useful contrast: if the instance refuses HTTP traffic but SSH works, that points to missing application-level configuration rather than network rules. Closing prompt: after you add an SSH rule, how would you prove the problem was fixed and not masked by another issue like a misconfigured internal firewall?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › SSH Troubleshooting
Quick checklist
  1. Confirm instance is ACTIVE: openstack server show <name>.
  2. Confirm floating IP is assigned and reachable.
  3. Inspect security group rules for TCP port 22.
  4. Confirm the key-name matches the private key used by the client.
  5. Check instance cloud-init logs for key injection failures.
Common contrasts
If SSH fails but HTTP works, the issue is likely the SSH rule or key rather than network reachability. If both fail, suspect security group or floating IP misconfiguration.
Common Mistake

Assuming a floating IP means SSH is allowed; you still need a security group rule allowing port 22.

Concrete example
If openstack server show reports the correct floating IP and the security group attached lacks a rule for port 22, run the security group rule create command to add SSH and re-test. If the issue persists, inspect the instance's internal firewall and cloud-init logs for the key injection status.
Validation step
After adding a rule, use a fresh SSH attempt from a known client and collect connection diagnostics. If the connection times out, re-check network routing and external ACLs.

screens.title: Glance: image repository and formats
screens.narratorSegment: Glance is the OpenStack Image service that stores virtual disk images used as templates to boot instances. Images in Glance can be public or private and come in formats such as QCOW2 and RAW. Choosing the right format affects flexibility and storage efficiency. QCOW2 is a copy-on-write format that supports snapshots, sparse allocation, and several advanced features; it is often preferred for its efficiency and snapshot support. RAW is simpler and may be useful for low-level compatibility but lacks QCOW2 features. You can upload vendor-provided cloud images or create your own by configuring an instance and snapshotting it back into Glance; when doing this, ensure the image is minimized and contains cloud-init to allow initial configuration and key injection. A common mistake is using outdated images or storing many slightly different images, leading to image sprawl and storage waste. The takeaway: manage a small, curated catalog of images and lean on QCOW2 when you need snapshots and space efficiency. Which image formats does your environment prefer and why? Glance: image repository and formats means prefer qcow2 for features and efficiency, include cloud-init for automated configuration, and maintain a curated image catalog to avoid sprawl.. In practical terms, what glance stores and why image format matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Glance Images
Image formats
QCOW2: supports snapshots, sparse files, and is space-efficient. RAW: simple and widely compatible but lacks snapshots and space-saving features.
Image lifecycle
Import vendor images or create your own by installing and hardening a system, then snapshot it to Glance. Keep images clean and include cloud-init for automation.
Key Takeaway

QCOW2 is usually preferred for images because it supports snapshots and efficient storage; manage images to avoid sprawl and stale templates.

Concrete command
# Upload a QCOW2 image to Glance
openstack image create "cirros" \
  --file cirros-0.5.2-x86_64-disk.img \
  --disk-format qcow2 --container-format bare \
  --public

# Verify
openstack image list
Common mistake
Using many slightly different images instead of parameterized configuration leads to image sprawl and storage waste. Standardize and patch images regularly.

screens.title: Importing and creating images in Glance
screens.narratorSegment: You can bring images into Glance by downloading vendor-provided cloud images or by creating your own image from a configured instance. The chapter shows downloading a small test image like CirrOS and uploading it with openstack image create, specifying disk and container formats. For production images, launch an instance, install only required packages, run security patches, configure cloud-init for first-boot tasks, then snapshot the instance and register that snapshot in Glance. When uploading, choose QCOW2 for snapshots and efficiency, and set visibility to public or private as appropriate for your tenant policies. A common issue is forgetting cloud-init, which prevents automatic SSH key injection and initial configuration. Another is uploading images with leftover user accounts or SSH keys; always scrub images before snapshotting. The practical takeaway: follow a documented image build process, include cloud-init, test boot behavior, and then mark the image with metadata that describes intended usage. How will your team ensure every production image includes cloud-init and a documented build date? Importing and creating images in Glance means build images from fresh installs, scrub secrets, include cloud-init, and add metadata to track purpose and build date.. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Image Import
Vendor image upload
# Example: download and upload a test image
# wget http://download.cirros-cloud.net/0.5.2/cirros-0.5.2-x86_64-disk.img
openstack image create "cirros" --file cirros-0.5.2-x86_64-disk.img --disk-format qcow2 --container-format bare --public

openstack image list
Confirm the image is listed before using it to boot instances.
Snapshotting your own image
Configure a clean instance, verify cloud-init runs correctly, remove secrets, then snapshot and upload to Glance. Add metadata tags describing purpose and build date.
Checklist before upload
  • Remove local SSH keys and user accounts you do not want shared.
  • Install cloud-init for first-boot configuration.
  • Patch and minimize installed packages to reduce attack surface.
Why it matters

A clean, well-documented image reduces operational overhead and security risk when used across tenants and projects.

screens.title: Image hygiene and lifecycle management
screens.narratorSegment: Good image governance prevents storage waste and security drift. Image sprawl occurs when teams keep multiple slightly different images for the same purpose. To prevent this, standardize on a small number of base images and use cloud-init for instance-specific configuration instead of baking every variance into separate images. Regularly patch images and keep a deprecation policy so older images are retired. Snapshot workflows are useful: create a golden image, test boots, then snapshot and tag with metadata including creation date and intended use. Cloud-init is critical because it enables key injection and first-boot scripts; without it you will struggle to automate instance customization. Another best practice is to mark images public only when necessary and use private images for tenant-specific builds. Finally, monitor storage consumption from Glance and prune images that are unused or outdated. A closing reflection: when you audit your image catalog, what criteria will you use to retire an image? Image hygiene and lifecycle management means standardize base images, use cloud-init for customization, tag images with metadata, and enforce a deprecation policy to control sprawl.. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Image Hygiene
Avoiding image sprawl
Keep a small catalog of well-documented base images. Use cloud-init to handle per-instance configuration instead of creating many near-identical images.
Lifecycle policy
  • Tag images with build date and intended role.
  • Schedule regular audits and deprecate old images.
  • Test boots before promoting an image to production.
Key Takeaway

Treat images as software artifacts: version them, test them, and retire them when obsolete to maintain security and efficiency.

Concrete checks
When an image is older than your patch window or is unused for a defined period, mark it for deprecation. Remove secrets and verify cloud-init before reuse.
Misconception
Snapshots are not a substitute for a reproducible image build pipeline. Keep a build recipe and automation to recreate golden images rather than relying on ad-hoc snapshots.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how Nova and Glance work together to deliver virtual machines from trusted templates. Nova orchestrates the lifecycle of instances — booting, stopping, and terminating — while Glance stores the disk images that we use as templates. You will see concrete commands for creating flavors, uploading SSH key pairs, defining security group rules, and importing images into Glance. Knowing how to design flavors and manage image formats matters because flavors determine runtime resource allocation and images determine boot behavior and security posture. A mis-sized flavor wastes host resources, and a stale image can expose vulnerabilities. Throughout the lesson you will practice common CLI patterns and a reproducible workflow for launching a secure web server instance. Expect hands-on examples that show how to create a custom flavor, add a key pair, open SSH and HTTP in a security group, and upload a QCOW2 image. By the end you should be able to reason about instance sizing, secure access, and image hygiene. Consider: what would change for a database workload versus a web workload when you pick a flavor and image?

These objectives spell out practical skills you should master as an RHCA working with Nova and Glance. First, you will master creating and managing virtual machine instances with Nova; that means you will be able to identify the lifecycle states of an instance and use CLI commands to boot, stop, and terminate safely. Second, you will configure and use flavors and key pairs to provision instances that match workload and security needs; this includes creating custom flavors and injecting SSH public keys so passwords are not necessary. Third, you will implement security groups to control network access to instances; this involves crafting rules that allow only the required protocols and ports and avoiding overly permissive rules. Fourth, you will manage virtual machine images in Glance including creation, import, and choosing the correct image format. For each objective you will see both command templates and a small mnemonic to help you remember the workflow. These are verifiable competencies you can demonstrate by launching and securing a sample web server instance.

This page describes measurable steps you can use to verify the learning objectives. For managing Nova instances, you will demonstrate the ability to list instances, show details of a running VM, and safely delete test instances using the OpenStack server commands. For flavors and key pairs, create a custom flavor and then prove it by launching an instance that reports the expected C P U and memory. For security groups, create a web-sg that permits only SSH and HTTP, then verify the instance rejects other ports. For Glance image management, upload a QCOW2 image, confirm it lists in Glance, and boot an instance from it. Each objective includes an explicit verification checklist so you can mark the competency as complete. These verification steps help translate concept knowledge into production-ready actions and provide evidence you can show in an RHCA practical scenario.

Nova is the OpenStack service responsible for managing virtual machine instances and their lifecycle from boot to termination. Concretely, Nova coordinates resource allocation on hypervisors, tracks instance metadata, and exposes CLI commands to create, rebuild, resize, shelve, pause, and delete instances. This responsibility matters because instance lifecycle operations interact with other services: images from Glance define the disk template, networks provide addresses, and block storage attaches volumes. A common misconception is that Nova alone provides disk contents; in reality Nova consumes images from Glance when booting and delegates the image lifecycle to Glance. For example, when you run a server create command, Nova requests the image, schedules the instance on a compute node that has capacity according to the flavor, injects the SSH key if provided, and applies security group rules. An example claim: booting a web server from a QCOW2 image with a custom flavor and injected key pair should produce a reachable instance that reports the expected C P U and memory. Misunderstandings often arise when users expect instance disk contents to be updated when the Glance image changes — that does not happen automatically; snapshots or rebuilds are required. Takeaway: Nova runs the lifecycle but relies on images, flavors, and network security to produce a usable instance. How will you confirm scheduling and resource allocation when you boot a test VM?

Flavors are named profiles that define virtual hardware for an instance: vCPU count, R A M size, and root disk size. OpenStack ships with defaults such as m1. tiny and m1. small, but production workloads often require custom flavors tuned to their needs. For example, a database server typically needs more R A M and possibly dedicated C P U, while a stateless web server can use a smaller flavor with shared C P U. When designing flavors you must map virtual resources to physical host capabilities so you do not overcommit beyond what the hypervisors and NUMA topology can support. A common mistake is creating flavors with resource sizes that cannot be satisfied by the compute fleet, leading to scheduling failures. Another misconception is treating flavors as billing labels only; in practice they directly influence performance and scheduling decisions. Concrete example: create a flavor named m1. medium-custom with 2 vCPUs, 4GB R A M and 40GB disk, then set hw:cpu_policy to dedicated if you need isolated CPUs. The practical takeaway is to standardize a small set of flavors that cover typical workloads, and document the performance expectations for each. How would you map an OLTP database requirement of high memory and moderate C P U to a flavor spec?

Let's walk through creating a custom flavor and verifying it. The commands you will run define R A M, disk, and vCPUs and then set optional properties like C P U policy. Begin by creating the flavor with the create command. Next, set properties when you need dedicated CPUs or other metadata that Nova will use for scheduling. After creation, verify the flavor exists with openstack flavor list and inspect details with openstack flavor show. A useful pro tip: document flavor names and properties alongside the expected workload so operators know which flavor to use for which service. A concrete example from the source creates m1. medium-custom with 4GB R A M, 40GB disk and two vCPUs, then sets hw:cpu_policy to dedicated. A common mistake is forgetting to set flavor properties after creating the flavor, so double-check with flavor show. Closing question: when would you prefer shared vs dedicated C P U for a service, and how would you validate host support for the chosen policy? Create a custom flavor (CLI walkthrough) means after creating a flavor, always validate with openstack flavor list and openstack flavor show to ensure properties were applied.. In practical terms, commands, verification, and a small pro tip. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Key pairs are a foundational way to secure SSH access to instances. Instead of using passwords, which are hard to rotate and easy to leak, you create an SSH key pair on your workstation and upload the public key to OpenStack. When you launch an instance with that key pair name, the public key is injected into the instance so you can SSH using your private key. The practical steps are: generate a key with ssh-keygen if you do not already have one; upload the public key using openstack keypair create --public-key path name; and list keys with openstack keypair list. A concrete example from the chapter uses ssh-keygen with RSA 2048 and uploads the resulting public key. A common mistake is not using the key pair name when launching the instance, or using the wrong private key when attempting to connect. Another pitfall is committing private keys to version control. After uploading, verify the key pair appears in the list and confirm the instance metadata shows the key name. Takeaway: key pairs enable automated, secure access without passwords. How will you ensure private key security when multiple operators need access?

Security groups are stateful firewall rule collections applied to network interfaces of instances. They control what inbound and outbound traffic is allowed and are essential for isolating workloads and enforcing the principle of least privilege. A typical workflow is to create a security group for a role — for example web-servers — and then add rules to allow port 22 for SSH and port 80 for HTTP from required addresses. The chapter includes commands to create a security group and add rules for SSH and HTTP. A common mistake is forgetting to attach the security group to the instance or assuming the default group allows inbound traffic; often the default blocks incoming connections. Another pitfall is opening broad CIDR ranges unnecessarily. A concrete example: create web-servers, add rules for TCP 22 and 80 from 0.0.0.0/0 only if you need global access; otherwise lock to management networks. Finally, validate by checking openstack security group show and then testing connectivity. Consider whether a management jump host would reduce your exposure instead of allowing universal SSH access. Security groups: rules that protect instances means use narrowly scoped security group rules and attach groups intentionally to instances; avoid overly broad access ranges.. In practical terms, stateful firewalls and common rules for secure services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Here is a full command sequence to launch a web server instance that combines image selection, flavor choice, key pair injection, and a security group. First ensure your desired image exists in Glance. If it does not, upload it. Next create or choose a flavor and key pair, and create a web-sg with SSH and HTTP rules. Finally, run the openstack server create command specifying image, flavor, key-name and security-group to launch the instance. After boot, use openstack server list and openstack server show to confirm status and networking details. A common mistake is omitting the key-name or security-group arguments, which either prevents SSH access or leaves required ports closed. Example demonstrates launching cirros with m1. tiny and a previously uploaded key. After the server is active, assign a floating IP if external access is required and verify connectivity. Takeaway: the server create command ties together the prior setup steps; missing any piece will affect access or resource allocation. Booting an instance: full CLI example means confirm image, flavor, key pair, and security group exist before running a single server create command to boot a usable instance.. In practical terms, image, flavor, key pair, security group combined into a launch command. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When a user reports they cannot SSH into a running instance with a floating IP, the most common cause is security group rules blocking inbound SSH. Start your diagnosis by verifying that the instance is ACTIVE with openstack server show and that it has the expected floating IP. Next, list the security groups attached to the instance and inspect rules with openstack security group show. If port 22 is missing, add the rule and retry. Another possibility is that the wrong key pair was used at launch; confirm the key-name in the instance metadata and ensure the client is using the matching private key. Less common causes include the instance's internal firewall blocking SSH or cloud-init failing to inject the key at first boot. Always check cloud-init logs inside the instance when possible. A useful contrast: if the instance refuses HTTP traffic but SSH works, that points to missing application-level configuration rather than network rules. Closing prompt: after you add an SSH rule, how would you prove the problem was fixed and not masked by another issue like a misconfigured internal firewall?

Glance is the OpenStack Image service that stores virtual disk images used as templates to boot instances. Images in Glance can be public or private and come in formats such as QCOW2 and RAW. Choosing the right format affects flexibility and storage efficiency. QCOW2 is a copy-on-write format that supports snapshots, sparse allocation, and several advanced features; it is often preferred for its efficiency and snapshot support. RAW is simpler and may be useful for low-level compatibility but lacks QCOW2 features. You can upload vendor-provided cloud images or create your own by configuring an instance and snapshotting it back into Glance; when doing this, ensure the image is minimized and contains cloud-init to allow initial configuration and key injection. A common mistake is using outdated images or storing many slightly different images, leading to image sprawl and storage waste. The takeaway: manage a small, curated catalog of images and lean on QCOW2 when you need snapshots and space efficiency. Which image formats does your environment prefer and why? You can bring images into Glance by downloading vendor-provided cloud images or by creating your own image from a configured instance. The chapter shows downloading a small test image like CirrOS and uploading it with openstack image create, specifying disk and container formats. For production images, launch an instance, install only required packages, run security patches, configure cloud-init for first-boot tasks, then snapshot the instance and register that snapshot in Glance. When uploading, choose QCOW2 for snapshots and efficiency, and set visibility to public or private as appropriate for your tenant policies. A common issue is forgetting cloud-init, which prevents automatic SSH key injection and initial configuration. Another is uploading images with leftover user accounts or SSH keys; always scrub images before snapshotting. The practical takeaway: follow a documented image build process, include cloud-init, test boot behavior, and then mark the image with metadata that describes intended usage. Good image governance prevents storage waste and security drift. Image sprawl occurs when teams keep multiple slightly different images for the same purpose. To prevent this, standardize on a small number of base images and use cloud-init for instance-specific configuration instead of baking every variance into separate images. Regularly patch images and keep a deprecation policy so older images are retired. Snapshot workflows are useful: create a golden image, test boots, then snapshot and tag with metadata including creation date and intended use. Cloud-init is critical because it enables key injection and first-boot scripts; without it you will struggle to automate instance customization. Another best practice is to mark images public only when necessary and use private images for tenant-specific builds. Finally, monitor storage consumption from Glance and prune images that are unused or outdated. A closing reflection: when you audit your image catalog, what criteria will you use to retire an image? Image hygiene and lifecycle management means standardize base images, use cloud-init for customization, tag images with metadata, and enforce a deprecation policy to control sprawl.. Here are three concise concepts to remember as you work with Nova and Glance. Nova manages the lifecycle of virtual machine instances, scheduling them to hosts, and coordinating networking and storage. Glance is the image repository that stores bootable disk images, which you should curate and keep patched. Flavors define the virtual hardware profile for instances; choose or create flavors that balance tenant needs and physical host capacity. These definitions are short but central: Nova boots and manages; Glance provides images; flavors define resources. Keep these relationships in mind when designing, launching, and maintaining cloud workloads. These three short concepts focus on secure access, image formats, and network protection. First, key pairs deliver secure SSH authentication without passwords; keep private keys safe and verify key injection at boot. Second, QCOW2 is the preferred image format for many use cases because it supports snapshots and is space-efficient; choose RAW only when compatibility or simplicity dictates. Third, security groups are stateful rules that control inbound and outbound traffic; follow the principle of least privilege and avoid opening unnecessary ports. Together these practices reduce attack surface, enable automated provisioning, and keep images manageable. When you prepare an instance for production, ask: is my image patched, does my flavor match workload needs, is access restricted to only required ports, and are private keys stored securely?
